chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the charity (sadaqat) of the People of the Covenant (Ahl al-Dhimmah) and what is taken from their poll tax (jizya) from the price of their wine, the meat of their pigs, and their dead animals. He said: 'The poll tax is upon them in their wealth; it is taken from them from the price of meat or wine. So whatever they take from them of that, its burden (of sin) is upon them, and its price is lawful for the Muslims; they take it as part of their poll tax.'

key_terms.أَهْلِ الذِّمَّةِ: People of the Covenant (non-Muslims living under Islamic rule)
key_terms.فَوِزْرُ ذَلِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ: So the burden (of sin) of that is upon them

ai.seo_question: Is the money taken from non-Muslims for poll tax (jizya) derived from wine or pork considered lawful for Muslims?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the jizya collected from Ahl al-Dhimmah often comprised the monetary value of their own forbidden consumables, such as wine and pork. The scholarly significance lies in the principle that the impurity (wazr) of the item remains with the owner, while the converted value becomes lawful (halal) currency for the Muslim treasury, illustrating the flexibility of fiscal jurisprudence in early Islamic governance. This ruling underscores the practical application of 'cleaning' impure assets through valuation, a concept vital to Shia fiqh of taxation.
